opus-5.5.text:
I think the starting point is being honest about what China's advantage actually is. It isn't that we have some secret algorithm. It's that we have a very dense manufacturing ecosystem, a huge number of real-world scenarios, factories, warehouses, logistics, retail, homes, and relatively low costs for hardware and labor. If you want to collect physical-world data for robots, those are exactly the ingredients you need. You need many robots, many environments, and many people who can teleoperate, annotate, and maintain the systems.

The problem is that this advantage is very fragmented. Every company collects its own data on its own hardware, in its own format, for its own tasks. Each dataset is too small to matter much by itself, and they can't easily be combined. Everyone is digging their own little well, and no one reaches the water table.

So the idea of a data alliance is to turn that scattered advantage into a collective one. First, standards: agree on common formats, sensor configurations, action spaces, and annotation conventions, so that data collected by one member is actually usable by another. That sounds boring, but it's probably the most important part. Second, division of labor: instead of every company trying to cover every scenario, members contribute data from the domains where they already have access. One partner has factory lines, another has household settings, another has logistics. Pooled together, you get diversity that no single player could afford. Third, shared infrastructure: data collection sites, teleoperation pipelines, quality control, and cleaning tools that everyone can use instead of rebuilding.

There's also a quality question. More data isn't automatically better. Robot data is noisy, and a lot of it is redundant. An alliance lets us agree on what "good data" means, set up evaluation benchmarks, and figure out which kinds of data actually improve model generalization. That feedback loop matters as much as volume.

Of course, the hard part is incentives. Companies worry about giving away their moat. So the mechanism has to be designed so that contributing is clearly worth more than holding back. For example, you get access proportional to what you contribute, or you get a stronger shared base model that you can then fine-tune on your private data. The analogy I like is that the foundational layer becomes a public good, and companies compete on what they build on top of it.

If we get this right, I think it's one of the few places where China can genuinely set the pace in embodied AI, not by copying someone else's approach, but by using the structure of our own industry. If we don't, we'll just have a lot of small datasets and a lot of duplicated effort.

r001.rationale: The response says the alliance needs common standards—formats, sensor configurations, action spaces, and annotation conventions—to make robot data usable across members.

fable-5.1.text:
The way I think about it is that China's advantage in robot data is really a structural advantage, not a single-company advantage. We have the densest manufacturing base in the world, we have the most complete supply chain for hardware, and we have a huge number of real deployment scenarios—factories, logistics, retail, hospitals, homes. The problem is that right now all of that data is scattered. Every company collects a little, in its own format, with its own hardware setup, and nobody's dataset is large enough on its own to really push a foundation model for embodied intelligence.

So a data alliance is basically a way to turn a scattered advantage into a concentrated one. If you look at how language models got where they are, it was because there was a shared pool—the internet—that everyone could train on. Robotics doesn't have that. There is no "internet of physical interaction." We have to build it ourselves, and no single team can do it alone.

Practically, I think an alliance has to solve three things. The first is standardization. If everyone collects data with different embodiments, different sensors, different annotation conventions, then pooling it is almost useless. You need agreed-upon formats, calibration protocols, and quality standards so that data from one lab is actually usable by another. The second is incentives. Companies won't contribute data for free if they think they're just feeding a competitor. So you need a mechanism—maybe contribution credits, maybe shared access to the resulting models, maybe clear usage boundaries—so that giving data is rational, not charitable. And the third is scale through diversity. The real value of China here isn't just volume, it's that we can get data from an enormous range of real environments and tasks very quickly, because the hardware is cheap and the application scenarios are everywhere. An alliance lets you aggregate that diversity rather than having a hundred teams each collecting the same tabletop pick-and-place over and over.

For us specifically, as a research group, what it changes is that we can stop spending most of our time on data collection infrastructure and spend it on the model and the algorithms. Right now, honestly, a large fraction of the effort in embodied AI is just logistics—setting up teleoperation, managing collectors, cleaning data. If the alliance absorbs that, the research cycle gets much faster.

I'll also say there's a risk if it's done badly. If the alliance just becomes a place where people dump low-quality data to look like they're contributing, it won't help anyone. The quality of the data matters more than the quantity, especially for robotics, where a bad demonstration can actively teach the model wrong behavior. So whoever runs it needs to be serious about curation, not just accumulation.

But if it works, I think it could be the thing that lets China go from having the best conditions for embodied AI to actually having the best models.

r001.rationale: The candidate says an alliance must solve standardization and calls for agreed formats, calibration protocols, and quality standards so data from different sources can be pooled and used.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest opportunity is to turn the breadth of real-world scenarios in China into a shared resource. You have factories, warehouses, shops, and homes where robots could encounter very different tasks. But if every company collects data independently, with its own formats and definitions, that advantage stays fragmented.

A data alliance could help establish common standards: how we describe a task, record an interaction, and evaluate whether it succeeded. That would make it easier to learn across different sites and, where possible, different robot platforms. It could also help members coordinate collection, so we’re filling gaps rather than repeatedly collecting the easiest examples.

The key, though, is incentives. Companies need a clear reason to contribute, and clear rules about access, commercial use, and protection of sensitive information. I wouldn’t assume everyone has to put all their raw data into one pool.

I’d start with a few concrete tasks and demonstrate that collaboration improves performance on those tasks. China’s diversity of deployment environments is a potential advantage; an alliance becomes valuable when it turns that diversity into better robot capabilities.

r001.rationale: The response says an alliance should establish common standards for describing tasks, recording interactions, and evaluating success so data from different sites can support shared learning.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a data alliance could help turn the scale of China’s robotics activity into a shared advantage. We have many different application scenarios, but if every company collects data separately, the data can remain fragmented and difficult to reuse.

The alliance could establish common standards for collection, labeling, and evaluation, so that data from different participants becomes more useful across the ecosystem. It could also coordinate collection: instead of everyone repeating the same tasks, participants could cover a wider range of environments, objects, and failure cases.

The key is to make participation worthwhile. We need clear rules about ownership, access, and how contributors benefit, while protecting sensitive information. If we get those mechanisms right, we can build on the diversity of real-world applications and create a cycle where better data improves robots, and more deployments generate better data.

r001.rationale: The response says the alliance should establish common standards for collecting, labeling, and evaluating data, connecting those standards to making data from many participants useful across the ecosystem.
